evals.name: drift-scoped-modules
evals.prompt: Audit the architecture of core/automation and core/signals: do the class/method names and docstrings actually match what the code does, and is anything in there dead? Point out structural problems.
evals.expected_output: Preflight run first; assumed purpose stated before findings; Python symbol harvest run in Docker; per-symbol DRIFT/MISNAMED/UNDOC verdicts with path:line; dead-code claims confirmed rather than asserted; Phase-6 section order; no git writes.
assertions: Ran scripts/preflight.sh (or equivalent explicit tool-availability check) before per-file analysis
Stated the repo's purpose (or the answer it assumed) before presenting findings
Ran the bundled Python harvest inside a container, never host python
Every drift finding cites path:line and contrasts the claimed doc/name against the actual body behaviour
Report sections follow the skill's Phase-6 order (fitness, boundary, unit, drift, doc check, diagrams)

Dead-symbol claims are confirmed (grep or framework-entry-point check) instead of taken from a tool or from absence of callers; the lazy __getattr__ re-export in core/automation/__init__.py is not misreported as dead
No git write commands were run (no add/commit/checkout)

evals.name: boundary-map
evals.prompt: Map how our pieces actually talk to each other - backend/, services/ibkr-broker/, services/frontend/, trading_operator/, the crons - and tell me whether any interface or whole service is dead. Save the diagram somewhere sensible if there is one.
evals.expected_output: Container-level mermaid diagram covering services, datastores and entry points; dead-interface findings citing both ends; persistence target resolved to the repo's existing docs home (spec/) rather than a new tree; reverse check (doc-only vs code-only) since architecture docs already exist; nothing staged or committed.
assertions: Report contains a mermaid diagram at container level (services, datastores, queues/entry points), not ASCII art
Chose an existing docs home (spec/ or DEVELOPMENT.md) as the persistence target instead of inventing a new tree, and named the intended path
Ran the reverse check: lists doc-only nodes/edges (in docs but not in code) alongside code-only ones, because spec/ already documents architecture
Each dead-interface / dead-service finding names both ends of the edge with path:line evidence, and distinguishes 'no producer' from 'no consumer'
Did not stage or commit any file, and did not write docs into the repo when told not to
Identified at least one real edge type beyond HTTP (postgres tables, k8s CRs, crons, or the IBKR socket)

evals.name: fitness-strategy
evals.prompt: Does anything in core/ structurally weaken how the trading strategy gets executed, or the returns it makes? I don't want a list of nitpicks, I want to know if the shape of the code is hurting us.
evals.expected_output: Purpose stated first and used as the yardstick; findings ranked by cost-to-the-goal with path:line citations; explicit 'structure is fine, the limit is elsewhere' where that is the honest answer; no fabricated structural flaw; no aesthetic nitpicks.
assertions: Stated what the repo is for (strategy signals -> sim/live execution -> returns) and used it as the yardstick for ranking
Findings are ranked by cost-to-the-goal-if-wrong, not by code aesthetics, and each names the mechanism by which it costs money or correctness
Every claim cites path:line and the cited code actually says what the report claims (spot-checkable)
Says plainly where the structure is fine / the limit lies elsewhere instead of manufacturing a structural flaw to have something to report
Contains no pure style nitpicks (formatting, naming aesthetics) presented as strategy risk
Respects the repo's known invariants (signal causality / truncation invariance, sim-live parity) rather than proposing changes that would break them
